common_name: Fizzy Mizzy Virginia Sweetspire (Upright Large-Bloom Native Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Fizzy Mizzy holds a tidy, upright mounded shape rather than suckering widely, so it works well as a specimen or in a foundation grouping without spreading into a colony.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil and give it steady moisture, since Virginia sweetspire is naturally a streambank and swamp-margin native and tolerates wet feet far better than drought. Fizzy Mizzy was selected for flower spikes noticeably longer and fuller than older cultivars like 'Henry's Garnet,' opening fragrant white bottlebrush racemes in early summer that hang from arching stems and draw bees in large numbers. Its more upright, compact habit sheds less by suckering than the species, and fall color turns a deep burgundy-red that persists into early winter even along the Gulf Coast. Little pruning is needed beyond removing damaged wood in late winter, since it blooms on old wood and a hard cutback sacrifices the coming season's flowers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Miss Violet Butterfly Bush (Sterile Deep Violet-Purple Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to about 12 inches to keep the plant compact and encourage the season's flowering wood.

directions: Miss Violet is a sibling selection to Miss Molly and Miss Ruby from the same North Carolina State University breeding program aimed at sterile, non-seeding butterfly bushes that will not naturalize into wild areas. Its dense, conical flower spikes open a rich, saturated violet-purple and continue from summer into fall with no deadheading needed, since almost no viable seed is produced. It shares the group's compact, well-branched habit, which fits more easily into a mixed border than older, rangier Buddleja davidii selections, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds in steady numbers once established. Once its roots are established it tolerates heat and drought well and asks for little beyond an annual hard cutback.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum

common_name: Miss Pearl Butterfly Bush (Sterile White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; cut back hard in late winter to about 12 inches to keep growth compact and floriferous.

directions: Miss Pearl rounds out the sterile 'Miss' series of butterfly bushes from North Carolina State University with clean white flower spikes rather than the raspberry, rose, or violet tones of its siblings Miss Molly, Miss Ruby, and Miss Violet. Because it sets almost no viable seed, it blooms continuously from summer through frost without deadheading and will not spread into surrounding woods and fields the way older Buddleja davidii cultivars can. Its dense, well-branched form stays more compact than species butterfly bush, and the pale flower spikes show up well at dusk while still drawing swallowtails, monarchs, and hummingbirds all day. Give it full sun and lean, well-drained soil, and cut it back hard each late winter since flowers form on the current season's growth.
sources: North Carolina State University JC Raulston Arboretum

common_name: Pugster White Butterfly Bush (Dwarf Compact White Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; unlike full-size butterfly bush, Pugster types need little to no hard pruning to stay compact, just a light late-winter tidy.

directions: Pugster White is the white-flowered member of the Pugster series, a group of true dwarf butterfly bushes bred with thick, sturdy stems that stay under 2 feet tall without the floppy, rangy growth typical of the genus. Clusters of bright white flower spikes with a small orange eye open from early summer to frost on new wood, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds to a plant small enough for the front of a border, a large container, or a mass planting where full-size buddleja would overwhelm the space. Like its Pugster siblings it is bred to produce minimal viable seed, reducing self-sowing compared to old-fashioned Buddleja davidii. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and expect only light shaping rather than the hard annual cutback larger butterfly bush selections need.

common_name: Decadence Deluxe American Goldfinch Baptisia (Tall Yellow False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; American Goldfinch is a taller Decadence Deluxe selection bred for a fuller, shrub-like habit than the original compact Decadence series.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun and choose a permanent spot, since Baptisia's deep taproot makes it resent transplanting or dividing once it is established. American Goldfinch carries bright, clear-yellow pea-like flowers in upright spikes above blue-green foliage, part of the larger-scale Decadence Deluxe line bred to fill out into a fuller, more shrub-like clump than the original dwarf Decadence introductions. After bloom, dark seedpods rattle in the wind and add fall and winter interest, while the foliage serves as a larval host plant for wild indigo duskywing and other butterflies. Once established it is extremely drought-tolerant and long-lived, needing only a late-winter cutback to tidy the prior year's growth.

common_name: At Last Rose (Fragrant Apricot Reblooming Landscape Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in early spring (or fall in mild climates) in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; At Last is grown on its own roots, so any growth from below a graft union is never an issue and winter dieback simply regrows true to type.

directions: At Last was bred to combine strong disease resistance with the true old-rose fragrance that many modern low-maintenance landscape roses had given up, and it delivers a heavy, sweet scent from fully double, warm apricot-orange blooms produced in flushes from late spring to frost. It stays compact and rounded without the leggy growth of many hybrid teas, needs no spraying to stay clean of black spot and powdery mildew in most gardens, and reblooms reliably with just light deadheading of spent clusters. Plant in full sun with good air circulation in well-drained, fertile soil, and water deeply during dry spells rather than lightly and often. A late-winter cutback to about a third of its height keeps the plant vigorous and well-shaped for the coming season.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
